title: David
hook: When the Ziphites betrayed David's location for the second time, delivering him to Saul's vengeful pursuit, they demonstrated something more devastating than military defeat: the fracture of covenant community itself. These were fellow Israelites, neighbors who shared the same God and the same promises, yet they weaponized intelligence against the anointed king-in-waiting. What transforms David's story from mere political survival into spiritual drama is not the giant he slays or the throne he eventually claims, but how he responds when he holds absolute power over the man who has tried to kill him—not once, but repeatedly. In the limestone caves of En-gedi, with Saul literally at his mercy, David makes a choice that defies every strategic calculation: he cuts the king's robe but refuses to cut the king's life. President Spencer W. Kimball taught that "God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs." David's restraint reveals the inverse truth—that we can become instruments of God's mercy even toward those who have forfeited any human claim to it. This week's study asks whether we have the spiritual courage to spare what we have every right to destroy.
